claims.text: HEA protective-coating wear resistance is primarily governed by a nanostructured dual-phase microstructure.
A nanostructured dual-phase microstructure enhances adaptive work hardening through phase-boundary pinning during wear.
Deposition techniques such as sputtering can produce fine, nanocrystalline dual-phase HEA coatings.
Controlled thermal annealing will induce modest microstructural coarsening and phase growth.
The as-deposited coating has an evenly distributed, fine phase-boundary network.
Phase boundaries in the as-deposited dual-phase microstructure obstruct dislocation motion.
The numerous phase boundaries promote dynamic adaptive work hardening during wear.
Annealing-induced microstructural coarsening reduces phase-boundary density.
Reduced phase-boundary density diminishes adaptive work hardening.
Diminished adaptive work hardening makes the coating more susceptible to material removal.
The annealed, coarsened coating will have a statistically significant increase in wear rate relative to the as-deposited coating.
The annealed, coarsened coating will exhibit lower hardness under dynamic load.
The annealed, coarsened coating will exhibit reduced frictional behavior associated with less adaptive work hardening.
The predicted effect should hold for coatings with similar alloy compositions and deposition conditions within the nanocrystalline regime.
Extremely coarse-grained samples or fundamentally different HEA chemistries may not follow the predicted trend.
